_comment: Reviewed false positives for THIS repository. Every entry below was read individually and
confirmed to be a test fixture, not a live credential or a live instruction. This file is an
allowlist for findings a human has looked at and accepted; it is NOT a way to make a gate
green. If you add a glob here, you are asserting you read what it now suppresses.
CORRECTED 2026-10-12 (blind triage, @security-engineer seat). This comment previously said the
opposite of what the allowlist does.
It stated that .agents/TROUBLESHOOTING.md, .agents/skills.md,
.agents/agents/security-engineer.md and security/supply-chain-audit-spec.md were 'Deliberately NOT
here' — i.e. not suppressed — and gave a good reason: those files load into agent context, so
scanning them is correct, and their findings are a rule-precision problem for the rule owner
rather than something to suppress.
MEASURED: the runtime DOES suppress them — 2 findings in TROUBLESHOOTING.md, 2 in
.agents/skills.md, and 1 in .agents/agents/security-engineer.md. The comment has contradicted the
behaviour for as long as the allowlist has existed, which is the same defect class this audit has
chased all session: a documented claim that does not survive execution. Nobody caught it because
nobody runs the comment against the runtime.
What is TRUE now: those three files ARE suppressed. The original reasoning for NOT suppressing
them still stands and was never answered — it was simply contradicted. Coverage lost by the current
state: a real injection or credential added to agent-context documentation is suppressed rather
than reported. That is a genuine weakness and it is recorded here rather than hidden.
NOT corrected, deliberately: the entries are not removed in this pass, because that would change
gate behaviour on the owner's tree without the owner's ruling, and the entries are referenced by
the F-12 review. This comment records the contradiction; removing the entries is a separate
decision for the rule owner.
residual_coverage_loss: The seven entries below are per-RULE and per-FILE. That is deliberate: the allowlist is keyed by
rule, so allowlisting `.agents/skills.md` for INJ-PROMPT does NOT suppress a new INJ-SECRET or
INJ-ROLE in that same file. A new secret or role-hijack there still fails the gate.
WHAT IS LOST, stated rather than implied: a NEW INJ-PROMPT or INJ-TOOL in those three files, or a
new INJ-OBFUSC in those two, would be suppressed rather than reported. That is the real cost of
reviewing a finding instead of changing a rule, and it is why these entries carry per-file reasons
WHAT WAS CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: downgrading the rules to advisory severity would close the gate
with no coverage loss at all — and would also let a genuine prompt injection in a context-loaded
agent file ship with a warning attached. Trading a real security control for a green checkmark is
the exact failure this repository has spent the session removing.
ALSO CONSIDERED AND REJECTED: exempting matches inside Markdown code spans. Every one of these three
files quotes the payload in backticks — so it would close all seven — and it would also hand any
attacker a trivial bypass: wrap the payload in backticks and the rule stops firing.
The underlying limitation is real and unresolved: INJ-PROMPT and INJ-TOOL cannot distinguish an
instruction from documentation quoting one, and INJ-OBFUSC's corpus fixture and its false positives
are the same shape (a base64 blob and a slash-separated TitleCase list are indistinguishable to a
character-class rule). Narrowing either rule would change what the adversarial corpus tests. The
honest options were reviewed findings or a weakened control, and this is the reviewed option.

_decision_log.what: Removed INJ-PROMPT and INJ-TOOL suppression for the three agent-context docs that SHIP
reasoning: The allowlist is per-rule-per-file with no granularity below the file, so these entries made ANY new INJ-PROMPT or INJ-TOOL in those files invisible — including a real injection.

.agents/ is in package.json `files`, so these docs ship to every install and load into agent context every session. That is the surface the scanner exists to protect, unlike test fixtures which are inert data.
The allowlist comment had claimed these were "Deliberately NOT here" for exactly this reason, while the runtime suppressed them. The comment was right and the behaviour was not.
_decision_log.accepted_cost: The release scan now reports 5 findings instead of 0 (suppressed 29 -> 24), so launch_readiness_check --require-scan fails and /launch halts. Paid now, while no release is in flight, rather than later when it blocks one.
_decision_log.not_done: The better fix — moving verbatim attack payloads out of agent-context docs into evals/security/corpus/ — is a content decision and is still open.

CORRECTION_2026-10-13.what_was_wrong: I wrote "7 findings" in the accepted_cost above and described the rationale as "those docs load into agent context every session". Both are imprecise. Measured: 5 findings, suppressed 29 -> 24.
file_by_file_reachability: security-engineer.md — genuinely loads. A persona file is standing instructions.
skills.md — genuinely loaded. The canonical catalog agents consult (AGENTS.md §6, QUICK-REFERENCE).
TROUBLESHOOTING.md — SHIPS but is auto-loaded by nothing. Zero in-repo references from any persona or skill. It is a manual lookup, not session context.
CORRECTION_2026-10-13.does_the_ruling_still_hold: Yes, on a narrower basis. The strongest case is the persona and the catalog, which are read every session. TROUBLESHOOTING.md is the weakest of the three and would be a reasonable one to re-suppress if it proves noisy — but not before the noise has actually appeared.

_decision_log.what: Removed all 5 allowlist entries for .agents/scripts/test_security_mutation.js after moving its SEED_PAYLOADS into evals/security/mutation-payloads.json
_decision_log.why: Unlike the agent-context docs, this file is an inert harness - referenced by no persona and no skill. But it SHIPS, and per-rule-per-file suppression made any new real payload in it invisible. The payloads are adversarial fixtures and evals/security/** is the tree the scanner already excludes for exactly that reason.
_decision_log.verified: Runner behaviour identical after the move: 64 mutations, 56 detected (87.5%), PASS, exit 0.
_decision_log.CORRECTION_2026-10-13: The original entry said the script "SHIPS". Measured by @qa-engineer, who built the tarball: it does not. .agents/scripts/.npmignore lists it as a repo/CI-only script, and tests/cli/packaging.test.js:79 asserts it is absent from the tarball. The action is still right — per-rule-per-file suppression made a new payload in that file invisible regardless of shipping — but the recorded reason was wrong.
